h1: Hardy–Weinberg from the Dominant Homozygote Frequency
summary:
Homozygous dominant frequency is p². It returns dominant allele frequency (p), recessive allele frequency (q), heterozygote frequency and recessive homozygote frequency, and the panel shows all of them at once.

Unless you have genotype-level data — sequencing, a codominant marker, a biochemical test — you cannot see this class, so it is usually used the other way round: to predict how many homozygotes a population should contain. Every result is derived from the boxes you fill in, so changing one input updates the whole panel at once. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Hardy–Weinberg from the Dominant Homozygote Frequency
sections.html:
p = √(p²); q = 1 − p; 2pq = 2p(1 − p)

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
p²homozygous dominant frequency0–1
pdominant allele frequency0–1
qrecessive allele frequency0–1

sections.title: How do I use the Hardy–Weinberg from the Dominant Homozygote Frequency?
sections.html:
The form asks only for what the formula needs — nothing is optional decoration.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: homozygous dominant frequency (p²) of 0.49.

Substituting them into the formula gives dominant allele frequency (p) of 0.7, recessive allele frequency (q) of 0.3, heterozygote frequency of 0.42, recessive homozygote frequency of 0.09.

The arithmetic is the page's own: change one box and the result moves by the amount the formula implies, which is the quickest way to convince yourself the tool is honest.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• This direction needs genotype data, not phenotypes: a dominant phenotype pools AA and Aa and hides the split.

  • Codominant markers such as microsatellites or SNP arrays give p² directly, which is why population studies use them.

  • The square root is exact only at equilibrium; selection and drift both distort it.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
The arithmetic is simple; the inputs are where things go wrong. The usual culprits:

  • Using the dominant phenotype frequency as if it were p².
  • Forgetting that the three genotype frequencies must sum to 1.

faq.q: What is p if 49% of a population is AA?
faq.a: p = 0.7, so q = 0.3 and 42% should be heterozygotes.

faq.q: Can I get p from a dominant phenotype?
faq.a: Not without extra information — that is why recessive traits are the classical tool for estimating allele frequencies.

faq.q: What does the Hardy–Weinberg from the Dominant Homozygote Frequency actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns dominant allele frequency (p), recessive allele frequency (q), heterozygote frequency and recessive homozygote frequency. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
